speaker: Patrick Hsu
title: Arc Institute's Patrick Hsu on Building an App Store for Biology with AI
question: In pharmaceutical R&D, why do senior budget holders often push back on AI tools focused purely on early drug discovery?
guest: If you talk to some pharma executives—not the drug discovery organizational leaders, but the budget people who hold the enterprise purse strings—they'll say, "Well, I don't spend actually that much money on drug discovery. I actually spend most of my money on drug development. So tell me something about drug development, which is really where most of my dollars go. How can AI help me with that?" I think that is a very deep comment, because it says something about where money is spent and where value can be found. The first thing to realize is our industry probability of success is like 10%. A lot of the things people complain about or comment on in drug discovery and development fall out of that fundamental statistic. Why does the FDA heavily regulate? Why is it so focused on safety? Well, if 90% of the time it doesn't work, they're going to care a lot about safety. The promise of AI is if we can go from 10% probability of success to 20, 30, or 50%.

points.core: Pharmaceutical companies spend most R&D dollars on clinical development rather than early discovery.
points.note: Accept: clinical trials/development consume the vast majority of pharma R&D budgets compared to early discovery/molecule design. Do not credit: generic claims that drug R&D is expensive without contrasting development spend against discovery spend.

points.core: Drug development suffers from roughly a ten percent overall probability of clinical success.
points.note: Accept: ~10% clinical probability of success (accept 5-15% range) or ~90% clinical failure rate. Do not credit: vague statements that drugs often fail without conveying the severe ~90% attrition rate.

points.core: High clinical failure rates force regulators to prioritize safety heavily over speed.
points.note: Accept: because ~90% of candidates do not work, the FDA/regulators structurally impose strict safety-first oversight. Do not credit: blaming regulatory bureaucracy without linking strict safety scrutiny to the high baseline failure rate.

points.core: Improving clinical success rates unlocks far more value than speeding up early discovery.
points.note: Accept: moving clinical POS (e.g., from 10% to 20-50%) creates far greater ROI than packing the top of funnel with more early molecules. Do not credit: generic praise of AI in pharma without tying value to raising clinical probability of success.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Senior budget holders tend to push back because early discovery is not where most of the cost, time, or risk in drug development sits. Finding a candidate molecule is rarely the bottleneck; the expensive failures happen in clinical development, where roughly 90% of candidates fail, mostly in Phase II and III due to lack of efficacy or safety problems rooted in incomplete understanding of human biology. Clinical trials also consume the majority of R&D spend and timeline.

So an AI tool that generates more hits or designs molecules faster simply feeds more candidates into the same clinical funnel without demonstrably improving the probability of success. Shaving months off a preclinical stage matters little against a ten-plus-year programme, and the payoff takes many years to verify, which makes ROI hard to prove within a budget cycle. So far, AI-discovered drugs have not shown clearly better late-stage success rates, and none has yet delivered a wave of approvals.

Budget holders therefore favour tools that address target validation, translational prediction, trial design, patient selection, and operational efficiency, where savings are larger, nearer-term, and measurable.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Senior pharmaceutical R&D budget holders push back on purely early-discovery AI tools because molecule discovery is neither the primary cost driver nor the true bottleneck in drug development. Clinical trials consume roughly two-thirds of total R&D budgets and most of a drug’s timeline, whereas hit identification and lead optimization represent a much smaller share. Simply generating preclinical candidates faster without improving human biological translation risks flooding the pipeline with molecules that still fail in costly Phase II and III trials, where nearly 90% of clinical assets wash out over efficacy or safety. Rather than cutting overall spend, a wider early funnel can actually inflate downstream wet-lab validation and clinical expenses.

Moreover, early-discovery AI offers a distant, hard-to-prove return on investment: commercial payoffs take a decade to materialize—far outlasting executive budget cycles—while demanding immediate outlays for proprietary data curation and experimental assay verification. Consequently, budget holders increasingly prioritize AI that raises clinical probability of success or directly compresses trial execution, such as patient stratification, protocol optimization, and site recruitment.

noweb.answer: Senior pharmaceutical R&D budget holders often push back on early-discovery AI tools because those tools optimize a relatively cheap, fast stage of the pipeline rather than its true economic bottlenecks. Clinical trials account for roughly two-thirds of total R&D spend and most of the development timeline, yet nearly ninety percent of drug candidates entering human studies still fail—primarily due to insufficient clinical efficacy or unforeseen human toxicity rather than an inability to find or design molecules. Generating virtual hits or novel chemical matter faster rarely improves overall clinical success rates when underlying target biology and animal-to-human disease translation remain poorly understood. Worse, flooding the early funnel with computational candidates can overwhelm downstream wet-lab synthesis, assay validation, and preclinical testing capacity, driving up near-term costs without producing better drugs. Combined with expensive proprietary data cleanup, workflow integration friction, and a multi-year wait before human readouts can prove return on investment, executives often view pure discovery AI as local optimization, preferring investments that de-risk target selection, patient stratification, or clinical trial execution.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Senior R&D budget holders usually push back because early discovery isn't where most of the money or risk sits. Discovery and preclinical work typically take only about a quarter to a third of the cost of bringing a drug to market. Clinical development takes the majority, and the most expensive losses come from Phase II and III failures, mostly because the drug doesn't work well enough or turns out to be unsafe.

Finding hits faster or designing molecules more cheaply saves money in the cheap part of the pipeline. Unless it also raises the chance that a candidate succeeds in patients, it can just send more weak candidates into costly trials. So far, AI-derived molecules have done well in Phase I but haven't clearly shown better Phase II efficacy success, so the promise of better compounds remains unproven.

Payback is also slow and hard to prove. A discovery tool's value appears only years later, after it has been mixed with many other factors. Tools aimed at clinical bottlenecks, such as patient selection, trial design, site selection, recruitment and biomarker strategy, are easier to justify because they affect the largest budget lines sooner and more measurably.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Senior pharmaceutical budget holders often push back on AI tools focused solely on early drug discovery because early-stage research represents a relatively small share of total R&D expenditure. The overwhelming majority of pharmaceutical R&D costs—and financial risk—occur in late-stage clinical trials, where most candidates fail due to human efficacy or safety issues. Accelerating hit identification or generating more preclinical molecules does not automatically improve clinical success rates; in fact, flooding the pipeline with additional candidates can inflate downstream validation and trial expenses without yielding better drugs.

Executives also face a severe attribution and timeline problem. Because it takes a decade or more for a newly discovered molecule to reach regulatory approval, the return on investment for early-discovery AI is difficult to prove within typical budget cycles. Meanwhile, wet-lab synthesis, biological validation, and clinical recruitment remain stubborn physical bottlenecks. As a result, leadership often prioritizes AI investments that reduce clinical trial costs, improve patient stratification, or de-risk late-stage attrition where measurable financial impact arrives much sooner.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Senior budget holders are judged on whether the R&D portfolio produces drugs that reach patients. An AI tool that generates more hits or designs molecules faster can save discovery time, but those gains only go so far if teams already have enough leads and the bigger bottlenecks are target validation, safety, or clinical efficacy. More leads can even add work if they require scarce lab capacity to validate.

The budget question is whether the tool helps teams make better decisions earlier. Can it help them drop weak programs sooner, select candidates with a better chance of reaching the clinic, or measurably cut the cost and time of reaching a development milestone? Those benefits can take years to verify, which makes a discovery-only tool harder to fund on the strength of benchmark results or predictions alone.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer: Senior budget holders care about the cost and probability of getting a drug to market. An AI tool may find promising molecules faster, but much of the spending and risk comes later, when teams must show that a candidate is safe and effective in humans. If clinical trial capacity is already stretched, finding more molecules may simply create a longer queue and more validation work. The investment case is stronger when a tool can show that it helps teams choose better candidates, stop weak programs sooner, or shorten a step that actually determines when a drug reaches patients.
